parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a driving school to book lessons.
script: Good morning, Kestrel Driving School, Megan speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hi. Good morning. I'm hoping to book some driving lessons. I've never been with your school before.
Of course. I'll take a few details from you now, and then we can look at times and prices. Can I have your name, please?
Sorry, could you spell the surname for me?
Thackeray. Lovely. And a contact number?
And your address? We keep it on the pick-up record. I'll need the postcode as well.
I'm at 14 Calloway Road, in Harbury. The postcode is HR3 8WN.
HR3 8WN. Thanks. Now, do you already hold a licence?
Yes, I got my provisional one last month. Until then I wasn't even thinking about driving, I used to cycle everywhere. But my new job is out of town, so the bike isn't really an option any more.
A provisional licence is exactly what you need to start, so that's fine. And have you had any practice behind the wheel at all?

A bit. My uncle's been taking me out in his car on Sunday mornings. I think it comes to about 20 hours, no, hang on, that includes all the time I spent in the passenger seat while he explained things. Actual driving, it's probably 12 hours.
12 hours, okay. That's a decent start for a beginner. We'd probably begin with an assessment lesson, and then the instructor can tell you how many more you're likely to need.
Now, when would suit you? We run lessons Monday to Saturday.
Well, I work shifts, so it's a bit awkward. Tuesdays I'm on the late shift, and Wednesdays are no good either because I have an evening class. Thursdays are fine, though.
Thursday, then. What time were you thinking?
I finish work at 3, so maybe 4 o'clock?
Let me have a look. Our instructors don't start the afternoon block until 4.30 on Thursdays, and the 4 o'clock slot is taken in any case. Would 4.30 work?
4.30 is fine. It'll give me time to get changed and grab something to eat.
Great. And where would you like to be picked up? From home, or somewhere else?
Could the instructor collect me from work? It's Fenwick Mill, on Dunmore Street. It's easier than going home first.
No problem at all. Fenwick Mill. I'll put that on the booking.
Thanks. Is there a car park there? I'd rather he didn't have to wait on the road.

I'll note it down for him, and he'll ring you when he's about five minutes away anyway. Now, let me tell you about the prices. A single one-hour lesson is 32 pounds. If you buy a block of 10, it's 290 pounds, which works out cheaper for each lesson. And there's a block of 20 for 540 pounds, which is the best value of all.
Hmm. 20 is a lot to commit to when I haven't even had the first one, and a single lesson seems a bit wasteful if I'm going to carry on. I think I'll take the block of 10 and see how it goes.
That's sensible. You can always top up later and still get the block price. So, a block of 10 for 290 pounds. We ask for a deposit of 50 pounds to secure the first slot.
Can I just pay that in cash when I come in for the first lesson?

I'm afraid we stopped taking cash at the office in January. You could pay by bank transfer, but that takes a couple of days to arrive, so I couldn't hold the slot until it does. Most people simply give a card number over the phone.
Okay, then let's do that. I have my card here.
Perfect. If you're ready, I'll take the number now. And I'll send you a text this afternoon with your instructor's name and a reminder of the day and time.
Brilliant, thank you. You've been really helpful.
You're very welcome, Daniel. We'll see you on Thursday.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A committee chair talks to villagers about the arrangements for a summer fete.
script: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming along to the village hall tonight. For those who don't know me, I'm Colin Marsh, chair of the fete committee, and I'll take about ten minutes to run through the arrangements for this year's Thornley summer fete, which takes place on Saturday 12 July. A lot has changed since last year, so please bear with me.

First, the venue. Those of you who've been before will know the fete is traditionally held on the village green. This year it can't be. Some of you have been saying the wet spring left the grass too soggy, and I'll admit I thought that was the problem too, but the real reason is the drainage work the council is carrying out there. The contractors won't be finished until August, so the green is fenced off. Instead we're using the school field, which the headteacher has very kindly lent us. It's a little smaller, but it's flat and it has a proper hedge all the way round, which should keep the wind off the cake stall.

Parking is the next thing people ask about. The church hall car park would be everyone's first choice, but the roof repairs mean it will be closed all summer. There's a bit of space behind the Fox and Hound, and the landlord has been generous, but he's asked us not to use it because of the brewery deliveries. So we've agreed something with Mr Dunmore, who farms on Mill Lane. He's letting us use the big field next to his farmhouse, it's about a five minute walk to the school, and we'll have signs up all along the lane.

Now, what's it all for? Last year we raised just over 3,000 pounds, and that paid for the new swings in the playground. This year our target is 4,000 pounds, and every penny is going towards a minibus for the Thornley Seniors' Club, so that members can get to hospital appointments and go on day trips without relying on lifts. A few of you suggested we should help with the village hall roof, but the Parish Council has found funding for that, so we can concentrate on the minibus.

As for entertainment, some things will be familiar and some won't. We tried a dog show last year, but only four people entered, so we've decided to drop it. We'd also have loved to hold a duck race on the brook, but the water level is so low in summer that the ducks would simply sit in the mud. So instead, thanks to Alan Pierce at the garage, there will be a display of vintage tractors in the top corner of the field.

Now, the stalls, because I know that's what you really want to hear about. I'll take them in the order you'll meet them as you come through the gate. First on the left is the cake stall, and as always that's in the safe hands of the Women's Institute. They'll be serving tea and coffee as well, so do bring a few coins. Next to that is the barbecue. I know the scout group usually does the sausages, but they're away on their summer camp that weekend, so the cricket club has volunteered, and they've promised to bring their own aprons.

The scouts haven't abandoned us altogether, though. The ones who aren't away have offered to run the children's games, so that's the coconut shy, the welly throwing and the egg and spoon race, down by the hedge. Then comes the book stall. The parents' association was going to take that on, but they have their hands full, so the Friends of the Library have stepped in.

After the books there's the plant sale. Our gardening club have been growing seedlings in their greenhouses since March, and I'm told the tomato plants are looking particularly good. And finally, near the exit, we have the tombola, which is being organised by the school parents' association. They have collected some excellent prizes, including a weekend for two in a country hotel, so make sure you buy plenty of tickets on your way out.

Finally, a plea for help. We still need about a dozen volunteers to help put up the marquees on the Friday evening, starting at six o'clock, and a few more to take down on Saturday night. If you can spare an hour or two, please leave your name on the sheet at the back of the hall. Thank you all very much, and I look forward to seeing you on the twelfth.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: A trainee chef and his mentor review a menu-planning assignment.
script: Come in, Liam, and sit down. I've had a look at your draft menu, and I thought we could go through it before you finish the write-up. Have you got a few minutes?
Yes, of course. Thanks for making time, Chef. I've been a bit worried about it, to be honest.

Don't be. Let's start with what the assignment is for. Some students think the college wants a costing exercise, and the costing does matter, but that's not the main point. What the examiners are really looking for is whether you can build a balanced three-course menu around what's actually in season. Prices and portion sizes follow from that.
Right. I'd got the idea that most of the marks were for the budget.
Some are, but fewer than you'd think. Now, you chose an autumn menu for forty covers. Tell me why.

Well, at first I thought I'd go for a spring menu, because I'd just been to the market and everything looked so fresh. But then I remembered my grandfather's allotment. He grew pumpkins and apples and all sorts of root vegetables, and I spent every October helping him dig them up. So I decided autumn felt more real to me. I could actually remember how things taste.
That personal connection comes through in the introduction, and that's no bad thing. How did the research go? Did you manage to visit any suppliers?

I rang three. The first one was really helpful about what's available, and the farm shop even let me talk to the grower. The trouble was the prices. I'd get a figure one week and then it would be different the next, sometimes by quite a lot, so my costings kept changing.

Welcome to the real world. Prices move with the weather and the harvest, which is exactly why professional kitchens review their menus every few weeks. For the assignment, I'd suggest you pick one week, state the date clearly, and use those prices throughout. Then add a table showing the cost per portion for every dish. It's much easier for the examiner to follow than a paragraph of figures.
Okay, a table. I can do that tonight.

Good. Now let's go through the dishes. Starter first. You've got cured salmon with a beetroot dressing. It's a lovely idea, and the colours will look beautiful, but salmon is expensive at forty covers. If your menu is supposed to sell at a moderate price, the starter will eat up too much of the budget. Have you thought about using mackerel instead?
Mackerel. Yes, that would be much cheaper, and it's local too. I'll change that.

Now the main course. Roast duck breast with a cherry sauce. Everybody loves duck, but think about service. It needs to be rested, and cooked to order, and when you've got a full dining room you simply don't have the time. Customers would be waiting far too long between courses.
I did wonder about that. I suppose I could cook it ahead and finish it in the oven?

You could, but then the quality suffers. Think about whether a braised dish might suit you better. Moving on. The pork belly. I like it, but let me count what's on the plate. Apple, fennel, cider, mustard, sage, and a hazelnut crumb. That's far too many flavours competing with each other. Cut it back to two or three and let the pork speak for itself.
That's fair. I got a bit carried away.

It happens to everyone. Dessert now. You've got a strawberry pavlova. It sounds delicious, but strawberries in October? They'd have to be flown in, which defeats the whole purpose of a seasonal menu. Why not use the pears you mentioned earlier, or the plums?
Yes, I see. I'd put strawberries because they're popular, but you're right. I'll rework it.

And finally the chocolate pot with the salted caramel. Honestly, I wouldn't touch it. It's simple, it can be made the day before, it costs very little, and it's the sort of thing people order without thinking. Leave it exactly as it is.
That's a relief. At least one thing is right.
More than one, Liam. Overall, it's a strong piece of work. Now, what's your plan for the next two weeks before the deadline?
I was going to ask a couple of my classmates to taste the new dishes and give me feedback. Or maybe email the supplier to check the final prices again.

Those are both reasonable, but I have a better suggestion. Cook the whole menu in the kitchen here, on a quiet Tuesday, and let the team have it as their staff meal. They'll tell you honestly what works and what doesn't, and you can note their comments in the write-up. That will impress the examiners far more than classmates being polite.
That's a brilliant idea. Would the head chef be happy with that?
I'll have a word with him. Let me know which Tuesday and I'll sort out the rota.
Thanks, Chef. I'll send you an email by the end of the week.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about animal camouflage.
script: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to look at one of the most striking features of animal life, which is camouflage. We tend to think of it as a simple trick, an animal that happens to look like its surroundings, but in fact it covers a whole family of strategies, each shaped by what predators or prey can actually see. So let's start with the idea that has dominated textbooks for over a century, background matching.

Background matching means that an animal's colour and pattern resemble the surface it rests on. The classic example is the peppered moth in Britain. Before the Industrial Revolution, most of these moths were pale, which made them almost invisible on lichen-covered tree trunks. As factories spread, the trunks became blackened with soot, and the pale moths were suddenly easy for birds to spot. Within a few decades, dark moths had become the majority. When air pollution fell in the twentieth century, the balance shifted back again.

But matching the background isn't always enough, especially for large animals, because a body has an outline, and the outline is what predators often recognise. This leads to the second strategy, disruptive colouration. Bold patches of contrasting colour, such as the blotches on a giraffe or the broken bands on some snakes, cut across the edges of the body, so that the eye no longer sees one solid shape. The aim is to break up the outline, and experiments with artificial prey have shown that these patterns really do reduce attack rates.

The third strategy deals with another problem, which is shadow. Sunlight comes from above, so the upper part of an animal is bright and its lower part is in shade, and this gradient makes any solid object look three-dimensional. Many animals, from sharks to deer, solve this by countershading. They are dark on the back and pale on the underside. When light falls on them, the two effects cancel each other, and the animal looks flat, almost as if it weren't there.

Now, camouflage doesn't always conceal. Take the zebra. For a long time, biologists argued about why a grassland animal would evolve stripes. Some suggested they confuse lions, but lions hunt mostly at dusk, when the pattern is hard to see anyway. A more recent idea is that the stripes are really aimed at a smaller enemy, biting flies. Experiments have shown that these insects find it harder to land on striped surfaces, so the pattern may protect zebras from disease rather than from predators.

Of course, the environment doesn't stay the same all year, and some animals have solved that problem by changing their coat. The snowshoe hare, found across northern forests, turns from brown in summer to white in winter. What triggers the change isn't the temperature, as many people assume. The hare's body responds to the length of daylight, so it begins to change before the first snow arrives.

If the hare is a slow changer, the cuttlefish is the opposite. A cuttlefish can alter its appearance in a fraction of a second. The skin contains thousands of tiny sacs of pigment called chromatophores, that's C-H-R-O-M-A-T-O-P-H-O-R-E-S, each of which can be expanded or squeezed by muscles under direct control of the nervous system.

Similar abilities are found in flatfish. A flounder lying on the sea bed will copy the grain of sand within seconds. In one well-known experiment, researchers placed flounders on an artificial surface printed with a checkerboard pattern. The fish did not match the squares exactly, but they produced a pale and dark mottled pattern that came as close as their skin allowed, which suggests they respond to the scale of the pattern rather than to its detail.

Not all camouflage depends on colour. Behaviour matters as well. Take the leaf insects of Southeast Asia, whose bodies have veins and even bite marks and brown patches that look like leaf damage. When they walk, they sway from side to side in a gentle rocking motion, just like a leaf moving in the breeze. If they walked normally, the disguise would collapse immediately, since predators are quick to notice movement that doesn't fit.

Finally, a special case. Mimicry is the strategy in which a harmless species copies a dangerous one. The best-known example is the hoverfly, which has no sting yet wears the yellow and black stripes of wasps. Birds that have been stung once tend to avoid anything with those markings, so the hoverfly benefits at no cost to itself.

To finish, I'd like to say a word about applications. Engineers are now studying cuttlefish skin to design adaptive fabrics that change colour in response to light, with potential uses in clothing and in military equipment. For next week, please read the chapter on warning colours, and bring your notes on the zebra experiments. Thank you.

passages.title: Life in the Dark: How Deep-Sea Vents Changed Our Ideas About Life
paras: A  Until the late 1970s, textbooks gave a tidy account of how life is fuelled. Sunlight was captured by plants and algae, and everything else, from grazing animals to the predators that hunted them, depended on that energy, directly or at one remove. The deep ocean seemed to fit this picture uncomfortably well. Below about 200 metres, sunlight fades, and below 1,000 metres it is absent altogether, so the sea floor was regarded as a cold, dark desert. Its few inhabitants were thought to survive on scraps, the slow rain of dead plankton and fish that drifted down from the bright waters far above.

B  In February 1977, a team aboard a research vessel working in the eastern Pacific lowered a small crewed submersible towards a ridge on the sea floor, some 2,500 metres down. The scientists on board were geologists, not biologists. They had come to study cracks in the volcanic rock, where hot water was suspected to be escaping. What they found instead was a thriving oasis. Around the shimmering water, clams as large as dinner plates lay in heaps, and crowds of pale crabs picked their way over the rock. Most striking were clusters of tubeworms, some more than two metres long, whose bright red plumes waved in the current. Nobody on the expedition had expected to find any animals at all, and the team had to improvise ways of preserving the specimens they collected.

C  The mystery was what these animals were eating. The answer lay in the water itself. Seawater seeps down through cracks in the ocean floor, is heated by molten rock below, and gushes out again laden with dissolved minerals and a gas, hydrogen sulphide, which is poisonous to most animals. Some bacteria, however, can harness the chemical energy locked in such compounds, using it to build sugars from carbon dioxide. This process is known as chemosynthesis, in contrast to photosynthesis. These microbes form the base of a food web that needs no sunlight at all. The tubeworms, which have no mouth or gut, house billions of bacteria inside a special organ and are fed by them. In return, the worm supplies the bacteria with the chemicals they need, which it carries in its blood.

D  Later expeditions found that vents are not rare curiosities but a global feature, occurring wherever tectonic plates are pulling apart or colliding. The most dramatic are the so-called black smokers, chimneys of mineral deposits that spew out water at temperatures above 350 degrees Celsius. The water stays liquid only because of the immense pressure at that depth. Not every vent is so hot. Others release cooler, clearer fluids that seep out for decades, and some are fuelled by chemical reactions between seawater and rock, with no volcanic heat at all. Each type of vent supports its own community, and the species found at one site may differ almost entirely from those a few hundred kilometres along the ridge. Over 500 species have been described so far, and most of them are found nowhere else on Earth.

E  The discovery forced scientists to reconsider where life might have begun. Vents offer many of the ingredients that early chemists considered necessary: a steady supply of energy, a rich mix of dissolved minerals, and tiny pores in the rock chimneys that could have concentrated simple molecules until they reacted. Some researchers now argue that life began not in a shallow 'warm little pond' but in such a setting, some four billion years ago. The hypothesis remains contested. Critics point out that the key chemistry has been reproduced only in part in laboratories, and that fossil evidence from this period is scarce and open to interpretation. Nonetheless, the idea has changed the conversation, and fewer biologists now assume that life must depend on sunlight.

F  The implications extend beyond our own planet. If living things can flourish on chemical energy alone, then icy moons such as Europa, which is thought to have a liquid ocean beneath its frozen crust, become far more interesting targets in the search for life. Space agencies have designed probes to analyse plumes of water erupting from such worlds, looking for the chemical signatures of the microbes found at vents. The vent communities have also proved a source of practical discoveries. Enzymes from heat-loving microbes, which work at temperatures that would destroy most proteins, are now used in industrial processes and in medical testing.

G  Yet the vents face threats of their own. Some of the mineral-rich chimneys contain copper, zinc and gold, and mining companies are exploring ways to harvest them. Scientists warn that removing a chimney could wipe out an entire community, many of which take decades to recover, if they recover at all. Vent ecosystems are also fragile because they are so isolated: a species lost from one site cannot easily be replaced from another. Several nations have proposed protected zones, although agreement remains elusive. Having changed what we know about life, the vents may now test how willing we are to protect it.

passages.title: The Cathedrals of Commerce: The Rise of the Department Store
paras: A  Before the middle of the nineteenth century, shopping in European and American cities was a haphazard business. Goods were sold from small specialist shops, a draper here and a hatter there, or from market stalls, and customers were expected to bargain over the price. Entering a shop often implied an obligation to buy, which discouraged casual browsing, and many middle-class women went shopping only when accompanied by a servant or a male relative. The department store, which emerged in the 1850s and 1860s, overturned almost all of these habits.

B  What made the new stores revolutionary was not size alone but a set of principles. Prices were marked on the goods and were the same for everyone, which removed the need for haggling and made it easier to employ inexperienced junior staff. Customers were allowed to walk in and look without being pressed to buy, and goods that proved unsatisfactory could be returned. Because the stores sold large volumes with only a small profit on each item, they could undercut their smaller rivals. One business historian has described the formula as the retailing equivalent of the assembly line, although the stores kept strict control over appearances: displays were rearranged every week and windows were dressed by specialists.

C  Architecture and technology played their part. Cast iron frames made it possible to build enormous interior spaces without bulky supporting walls, and large sheets of plate glass, which had become affordable, let daylight flood in and showed the goods to people in the street. Hydraulic and later electric lifts carried customers between floors, and by the 1890s many stores had electric lighting, which removed the danger of fire that gas lamps had posed. Aldermere & Pratt, which opened in 1869 and was among the first to be built for the purpose, had a glass-roofed central hall six storeys high, and visitors were said to come simply to look at the building. Its owners understood that the setting itself was a form of advertising, and they spent as much on marble staircases and ornamental fountains as on stock.

D  The stores also transformed the experience of being a customer. Tea rooms, reading rooms and ladies' cloakrooms gave women a respectable place to spend a whole day in town, a rarity at a time when few public spaces were considered suitable for them. Stores held seasonal sales, concerts and exhibitions. Some offered free delivery, and mail-order catalogues extended their reach to rural families who might never visit a city. Sociologists have argued that the stores taught people to see shopping as a form of leisure, an entertainment, rather than a chore. Newspaper columnists complained that they encouraged women to buy things they did not need, and a few commentators even claimed that the temptations of the shop floor were a danger to public morals.

E  Behind the glamour lay a workforce whose conditions were often harsh. Shop assistants, many of them young and unmarried, commonly worked more than twelve hours a day, were fined for minor mistakes, and in many stores were required to live in dormitories above the shop, where meals and curfews were set by the employer. Wages were low but could be boosted by commission, which encouraged assistants to compete with one another. From the 1890s, campaigns by assistants' unions and social reformers led to early closing laws and the Saturday half-holiday in several countries.

F  Smaller retailers did not accept the new competition passively. Many formed associations, lobbied for special taxes on large stores, and in a few cities organised boycotts or even demonstrations that ended in broken windows. Others responded by specialising, offering expertise and personal attention that a department store could not match. In most cases small shops did not disappear. Many survived by serving the immediate neighbourhood, where customers valued convenience and credit extended by a shopkeeper who knew them. Even so, the largest department stores grew rapidly, and by 1900 some employed several thousand people. Their buyers travelled to factories and fairs across several continents, and their own workshops produced everything from furniture to uniforms. The department store was therefore not only a place to shop but a major employer and an influential force in the wider economy of the cities that housed it.

G  The twentieth century brought both the peak and the decline of the department store. The spread of car ownership allowed families to live further from city centres, and from the 1950s, customers were drawn away by out-of-town shopping centres with free parking. Discount chains and later online retailers took further business. Many famous names have closed. A few have reinvented themselves, adding restaurants, beauty services and events to their offer, much as the early founders did. They are discovering again that what they sell is not simply goods but an occasion.

passages.title: Can Cities Be Designed for Happiness?
paras: A  Over the past decade, a growing number of mayors have announced that their cities will be judged not only by economic output but by the wellbeing of the people who live in them. Consultancies have produced indexes of urban happiness, conferences have been convened, and planners are frequently urged to design streets, squares and housing with joy as an explicit goal. The ambition is attractive, and I have no wish to mock it. But the claims being made are sometimes far ahead of the evidence, and it is worth asking what, if anything, a city's physical form can really do for the mood of its inhabitants.

B  The most frequently cited evidence concerns green space. Study after study has found that people who live near parks, trees or water report lower stress and greater life satisfaction than those who do not. It is tempting to conclude that building more parks will make people happier, and some advocates do exactly that. Yet the studies are, almost without exception, observational. Wealthier and healthier people can afford to live in leafy districts, and people who are already contented may be more inclined to walk to a park and therefore to notice and value it. Until researchers can follow residents before and after a new park opens, the direction of causation remains uncertain. I suspect that the true effect is real but considerably smaller than the headlines suggest.

C  A second popular belief holds that density is the enemy of happiness: that the tower block is inherently alienating and the suburban house with a garden the ideal. This view has a long pedigree, but the evidence is thinner than it appears. Much of the unhappiness attributed to density is really the result of noise, poor maintenance, and a lack of shops and services nearby, none of which is inevitable in a crowded neighbourhood. Some of the world's most densely populated districts are also among the most sociable, because their residents pass one another daily on foot, share staircases and courtyards, and sustain a street life that low-density suburbs, where nearly every journey is made by car, struggle to produce. Density, then, is not a problem in itself. It is an opportunity that can be squandered, and the quality of the design decides which outcome follows.

D  Part of the difficulty lies in how happiness is measured. Most city rankings depend on surveys that ask residents to rate their life satisfaction on a scale from one to ten. Answers to such questions are strongly influenced by the weather, the news and the respondent's mood on the day, and they differ systematically between cultures, with some populations reluctant to give high scores to anything at all. I would place more trust in indicators gathered over many years, such as the proportion of residents who stay in a neighbourhood once they can afford to leave, or the rate at which older people continue to live independently. These measures are crude, but they reflect what people do rather than what they say.

E  There is also the awkward question of whose happiness is being designed for. Averages conceal as much as they reveal, and a scheme that delights the typical respondent may do little for children, disabled people or the elderly. Worse, improvements can undermine their own purpose. When a street is closed to traffic and planted with trees, nearby property tends to rise in value, and the tenants who stood to gain most from the improvement may find themselves priced out of it. Planners who fail to anticipate this risk making a city happier on paper by replacing its less fortunate residents.

F  If physical form matters, I suspect it matters mainly because it shapes social life. The sociologist's phrase 'third places' describes locations, neither home nor workplace, where people meet neighbours without any obligation: the library, the market, the cafe, the public swimming pool. Such places are cheap compared with grand schemes, and their effects on loneliness are easier to demonstrate. Yet many have been closed or privatised under budget pressure. A council that wants to improve the wellbeing of its residents could do worse than to reverse these closures before commissioning any new landmark.

G  None of this means that cities should abandon the pursuit of wellbeing. It means they should pursue it with humility. No blueprint exists for a happy city, and I doubt that one ever will, since people's needs differ and change. A more realistic aim is to remove the well-documented sources of misery: long commutes, constant noise, unsafe streets, and housing that is too expensive or insecure. Happiness itself may then be left to the people who live there, who have always been rather better at finding it than the professionals who plan for them. That seems to me a more honest and more durable ambition than any promise of a city built for joy.
